steps.tx: A **cubitus varus** deformity represents the most frequent late structural complication of pediatric supracondylar humeral fractures. It arises from imperfect reduction where the distal condylar fragment unites with persistent medial tilt and internal rotation. The normal physiological carrying angle of ten to fifteen degrees valgus is lost, causing the extended forearm to deviate medially into a gunstock configuration.
steps.say: Cubitus varus or gunstock deformity is the commonest late complication of supracondylar fractures in children. It results from coronal tilt and internal rotation during healing. The normal physiological valgus angle flips into an inward tilt when the elbow extends.

vis.title: Carrying Angle Parameters
rows: Negative angle of minus 5 to minus 20 degrees
Coronal medial tilt with rotatory collapse
Physeal arrest is rare under 2 percent

steps.tx: Compare the two arms before reading the labels, because the carrying angle difference is visible at a glance. In **cubitus varus**, the forearm deviates toward the midline when the elbow is extended, reversing the normal outward angle and giving the gunstock appearance. The deformity is mainly cosmetic in mild cases but records a malunited supracondylar fracture behind it. Documenting the angle against the uninjured side turns an impression into a measurement that follow up can track.
steps.say: Cubitus varus turns the forearm inward at the extended elbow, reversing the normal carrying angle into a gunstock shape. Comparing with the normal side turns impression into measurement.

steps.tx: The critical **pathomechanical mechanism** involves coronal malalignment rather than growth plate arrest. Because the distal humeral physis contributes only twenty percent of longitudinal humeral growth, progressive physeal arrest is exceedingly uncommon. Instead, medial tilting of the distal fragment creates immediate static varus that remains fixed throughout remaining skeletal maturation without progressive angular worsening.
steps.say: The deformity stems from static bone malunion rather than growth plate damage. Because the lower humeral growth plate accounts for only twenty percent of arm growth, the angle does not get progressively worse as the child grows. It stays constant at the degree of initial malunion.

right.title: Physeal Integrity
points: Distal physis accounts for 20 percent growth

steps.tx: The diagnostic **three bony points** relationship remains intact despite striking visual deformity. In ninety degrees of elbow flexion, the medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and olecranon tip form their normal symmetrical isosceles triangle, and in extension, they lie in a straight line. This preservation conclusively differentiates extra-articular supracondylar malunion from traumatic elbow joint dislocation or condylar epiphyseal fractures.
steps.say: Even with obvious cosmetic deformity, the three bony points relationship of the elbow stays normal. The medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and olecranon tip form an isosceles triangle at ninety degrees flexion and a straight line in extension. That proves the elbow joint itself is anatomically intact.

steps.tx: The **French osteotomy** serves as the standard corrective surgical technique when severe deformity justifies cosmetic intervention. The surgeon removes a lateral closed bony wedge from the distal humeral metaphysis proximal to the olecranon fossa, leaving the medial periosteal hinge intact to prevent translation. Fixation using two crossed Kirschner wires or a low-profile lateral locking plate maintains correction.
steps.say: When corrective surgery is needed, the French lateral closing wedge osteotomy is standard. The surgeon removes a lateral bone wedge above the olecranon fossa while keeping the medial periosteum intact as a stabilizer. Two crossed wires or a small plate hold the corrected valgus alignment.

steps.tx: A key **clinical trap** is operating on a stiff joint before full range of motion is regained. Corrective osteotomy must be deferred until at least six to twelve months after the initial fracture, once mature bony consolidation and full flexion-extension arc are documented. Secondary ulnar nerve neuropathy or posterolateral rotatory instability may emerge decades later from altered elbow kinematics.
steps.say: Never operate on a stiff elbow. Wait at least six to twelve months until bone has fully consolidated and the child has regained full flexion and extension. Operating too early on an inflamed joint causes permanent stiffness. Also remember that tardy ulnar nerve palsy can develop decades later.

quiz.q: What is the primary cause of cubitus varus following supracondylar fracture in children?
options: Malunion with coronal medial tilt and internal rotation
Complete premature closure of the distal humeral physis
Trochlear avascular necrosis with medial collapse
Volkmann contracture of the forearm flexor compartment
quiz.explain: Cubitus varus is caused by malunion of the distal fragment with coronal medial tilt and internal rotation, not by physeal arrest.

quiz.q: Which clinical sign confirms that cubitus varus is a supracondylar deformity rather than an elbow dislocation?
options: Preserved isosceles triangle of epicondyles and olecranon
Presence of an anterior humeral fat pad sign
Disruption of the radiocapitellar alignment line
Permanent loss of twenty degrees of elbow flexion
quiz.explain: In supracondylar malunion, the three-point relationship formed by the medial epicondyle, lateral epicondyle, and olecranon tip remains intact, differentiating it from an articular dislocation.
